question: Do creatures phasing back in trigger enter the battlefield abilities?
answer:
No. When a creature phases back in (phases in), that event does not trigger "enters the battlefield" abilities. Rule [702.26d] explicitly states that the phasing event doesn't actually cause a permanent to change zones, even though it's treated as not being on the battlefield while phased out, and "Zone-change triggers don't trigger when a permanent phases in or out." Since enters-the-battlefield abilities are a type of zone-change trigger (as defined in [603.6a]), they specifically require the permanent to actually move into the battlefield zone — phasing in is not such a move.

When a permanent phases in, its status simply changes to "phased in" and the game once again treats it as though it exists [702.26c], but this is not treated as the permanent entering the battlefield for purposes of any effects that check its history, per [702.26d]. Similarly, if the phased-out permanent was an Aura, Equipment, or Fortification, abilities that trigger on attaching or unattaching don't trigger from phasing either [702.26j].

This holds true whether the phasing was caused by the normal phasing static ability during the untap step [702.26a, 502.1, 703.4a] or by a one-shot effect that phases a permanent out "until" some event, which later phases it back in [610.4, 610.4a, 610.4c] — none of these phase-in events are zone changes, so none of them trigger enters-the-battlefield abilities.

Zone-change triggers don’t trigger when a permanent phases in or out. Tokens continue to exist on the battlefield while phased out. Counters and stickers remain on a permanent while it’s phased out. Effects that check a phased-in permanent’s history won’t treat the phasing event as having caused the permanent to leave or enter the battlefield or its controller’s control.

question: how does trample work with deathtouch?
answer:
When a creature has both trample and deathtouch, the attacking player only needs to assign 1 point of damage to each blocking creature (not damage equal to its full toughness) for that damage to count as "lethal," and can then send all the remaining damage through to the defending player, planeswalker, or battle.

Here's why: Trample [702.19a] is a static ability that changes how an attacking creature assigns combat damage — the controller of an attacking creature with trample [Trample] must first assign at least lethal damage to each blocking creature before assigning any excess damage to the player, planeswalker, or battle it's attacking [702.19b]. Normally "lethal damage" for a blocking creature means damage at least equal to its toughness (minus damage already marked and damage arriving simultaneously from other sources) [702.19b].

Deathtouch [Deathtouch] changes what counts as lethal for this purpose: rule 702.2c states that any nonzero amount of combat damage assigned to a creature by a source with deathtouch is considered to be lethal damage for the purpose of determining excess damage. This applies specifically to the trample-assignment math in 702.19b, since 702.19b says to take into account damage already marked and damage from other creatures being assigned in the same step, but treats deathtouch's 'any damage is lethal' rule as one of the relevant factors for what counts as 'assigned lethal damage.' Rule 120.4a reinforces this for the general damage-excess calculation: any amount of damage greater than 1 is excess damage if the source has deathtouch.

So in practice: if a creature has trample and deathtouch and is blocked by one or more creatures, its controller can assign just 1 damage to each blocking creature (satisfying the lethal-damage requirement because of deathtouch) and then assign all remaining damage to the defending player, planeswalker, or battle being attacked. The attacker isn't required to assign only 1 — they could assign more to a blocker if they choose — but they aren't forced to assign toughness-based lethal amounts.

Once that 1 (or more) point of deathtouch damage is dealt to a creature with toughness greater than 0, that creature is destroyed as a state-based action [702.2b, 704.5h], regardless of whether the total damage marked on it reaches its toughness [120.6]. This deathtouch-destruction rule applies no matter what zone the damage came from [702.2d], though if the source is no longer around when the SBA check happens, last-known-information is used to determine if it had deathtouch [702.2e]. Having multiple instances of deathtouch or trample on the same creature doesn't change any of this — they're simply redundant [702.2f, 702.19g].

Note: if the attacking creature also has trample over planeswalkers and is attacking a planeswalker, a similar but distinct rule applies (702.19c) — damage must be lethal to blockers (1 point each, given deathtouch) and then damage up to the planeswalker's loyalty before excess can go to the planeswalker's controller — but that's a different keyword than plain trample.

This answer holds regardless of table size (two-player or multiplayer), since these are rules about damage assignment to blockers and the defending player/planeswalker/battle, not about choosing among multiple opponents.

question: is storm a triggered ability that can be countered?
answer:
Yes, Storm is a triggered ability that functions on the stack, and like other triggered abilities on the stack it can be countered — but only by an effect that specifically counters abilities, not by something that only counters spells.

Rule [702.40a] defines Storm: "When you cast this spell, copy it for each other spell that was cast before it this turn. If the spell has any targets, you may choose new targets for any of the copies." This is a triggered ability, matching the general form described in [603.1] and [113.3c] ("[When/Whenever/At] [trigger condition], [effect]"). If a spell has multiple instances of Storm, each one triggers and goes on the stack separately [702.40b].

Once the Storm ability triggers, it's put on the stack as its own object (not a spell) the next time a player would receive priority [603.3]. Rule [113.9] is explicit on this point: "Activated and triggered abilities on the stack aren't spells, and therefore can't be countered by anything that counters only spells. Activated and triggered abilities on the stack can be countered by effects that specifically counter abilities." So a card that says "counter target spell" cannot stop a Storm trigger, but a card or ability that says "counter target ability" (or specifically targets/counters triggered abilities) can.

One nuance: even if the Storm trigger itself is countered before it resolves, the spell that has Storm was already cast and is separately on the stack; countering the Storm trigger only stops the copying effect, it does not by itself counter the original spell.

question: can i use cards with hybrid mana symbols in a commander deck that only has one of those colors?
answer: No — a card containing a hybrid mana symbol counts as being *both* of that symbol's colors for color-identity purposes, so it can't go into a Commander deck whose commander's color identity has only one of those colors, even though you'd only ever pay one half of the symbol when casting it. Rule 107.4e states that "a hybrid mana symbol is all of its component colors," and rule 202.2d confirms an object with a hybrid mana symbol "is all of the colors of those mana symbols." Since rule 903.4 defines a card's color identity as the color or colors of any mana symbols in its mana cost or rules text, a card with, say, {R/G} in its cost has both red and green in its color identity — it doesn't matter that you could choose to pay it with only red mana (per rule 118.7e/106.8, the choice of which half to pay is a payment mechanic, not a color-identity mechanic). Rule 903.5c then requires that every color in a card's color identity also be in the commander's color identity. So a card with {R/G} can only be included in a Commander deck whose commander's color identity includes both red and green — it cannot go in a mono-red or mono-green commander's deck. This holds the same way at any table size, since color identity and deck-construction legality (903.5c) aren't affected by how many players are in the game.

question: can I respond to the untap step?
answer:
No. During the untap step, no player receives priority, so you cannot cast spells or activate abilities to "respond" to anything happening in that step. Rule [502.4] states plainly: "No player receives priority during the untap step, so no spells can be cast or resolve and no abilities can be activated or resolve." This is one of only two kinds of steps where no one gets priority at all (the untap step and certain cleanup steps), per [500.3].

What happens during the untap step is entirely turn-based actions with no stack interaction: phasing occurs first ([502.1]/[703.4a]/[702.26a]), then the day/night check if applicable ([502.2]/[703.4b]/[731.2]), and finally the active player untaps their permanents ([502.3]/[703.4c]). None of this uses the stack, and per [500.12] no game events can occur between steps, phases, or turns, so there's no window to squeeze in a response mid-step either.

If something triggers during the untap step (for example, a "phases out" or "doesn't untap" trigger), that triggered ability doesn't go on the stack immediately - it's held until the next time a player would receive priority, which is normally the upkeep step. At that point, per [503.1]/[503.1a], the active player gets priority, and any abilities that triggered during the untap step (along with any that trigger at the beginning of upkeep) are put on the stack first, in any order, before the active player receives priority. That's your first opportunity to respond to anything related to the untap step - during the upkeep step, not the untap step itself.

This holds the same whether it's a two-player game or a multiplayer game - the rules cited here describe the untap step by reference to "the active player" and "a player," and nothing in these rules changes based on how many players are at the table.

question: are creatures still considered attacking creatures during the end of combat step?
answer:
Yes. A creature remains an attacking creature throughout the end of combat step, and only stops being an attacking creature when it's removed from combat (for reasons like leaving the battlefield, changing controller, phasing out, etc. — see the removed-from-combat conditions) or when the combat phase itself ends, whichever happens first. The end of combat step is the fifth and final step of the combat phase, not something separate from it, so simply reaching that step does not end a creature's attacking status. Per the glossary definition of "Attacking Creature," a creature declared as an attacker (or put onto the battlefield attacking) remains an attacking creature until it's removed from combat or the combat phase ends, whichever comes first [Attacking Creature]. The end of combat step has no turn-based actions that remove creatures from combat — the active player simply receives priority [511.1]. It's only *as soon as the end of combat step ends* that all creatures, battles, and planeswalkers are removed from combat, and only after that does the combat phase conclude and the postcombat main phase begin [511.3]. So during the end of combat step itself, attacking creatures (as declared per 508.1k, or put onto the battlefield attacking per 508.4) are still attacking creatures; they cease to be attacking creatures at the very end of that step, when the phase transitions.

Note: if something specifically removes a creature from combat during the end of combat step (e.g., it leaves the battlefield, changes controller, phases out, etc.), it stops being an attacking creature at that point per the removed-from-combat rule [506.4], even before the step ends normally.

This answer holds regardless of player count, since nothing about the number of players affects when creatures stop being attacking creatures.

question: Do you cast lands?
answer: No. A land card is never cast as a spell—it is "played," which is a special action, not the casting of a spell. Per rule [305.1], a player who has priority may play a land card from their hand during a main phase of their turn when the stack is empty; playing a land is a special action, so it doesn't use the stack, and since it never goes on the stack, it is never a spell. Rule [701.18a] confirms that to play a land means to put it onto the battlefield from the zone it's in (usually the hand), and this doesn't use the stack—it simply happens. Rule [116.2a] similarly lists playing a land among the special actions a player can take. Because a land is never cast, it can't be countered and players can't respond to the act of playing it with instants or activated abilities [505.6b]. This distinction matters even for cards that are both a land and another card type (like artifact lands): per [300.2a] and [305.9], such an object can only be played as a land—it can't be cast as a spell, even though the "other" card type (e.g., artifact) would normally be cast. The term "play a card" is broader and means either playing a card as a land or casting it as a spell, whichever is appropriate [701.18b], but lands specifically are always played, never cast. This rule is the same whether the game has two players or more than two; none of the provided rules indicate any multiplayer-specific difference in whether lands are cast versus played.

question: can I sacrifice an evoked creature before that creature's evoke triggered ability resolves?
answer:
Yes. Evoke creates two separate abilities: a static ability that lets you cast the creature for its evoke cost, and a triggered ability that reads "When this permanent enters, if its evoke cost was paid, its controller sacrifices it" [702.74a]. That triggered ability goes on the stack when the creature enters the battlefield, and players get priority before it resolves. During that window, you (or an opponent, if they control a relevant sacrifice outlet you've granted them, though normally only you can sacrifice your own permanent) can use another sacrifice ability or effect to sacrifice the evoked creature before the evoke trigger itself resolves.

If the creature is already gone from the battlefield by the time the evoke trigger tries to resolve, the instruction "its controller sacrifices it" simply can't be carried out — there's no permanent left to sacrifice. Rule 608.2d confirms that when a resolving ability calls for an action, a player can't choose (or, in this mandatory case, perform) an option that's illegal or impossible; sacrificing something that no longer exists is impossible, so that part of the ability just does nothing. The creature won't be sacrificed a second time, and no other effect substitutes for it, since each payment or cost/instruction applies only to the ability that created it [118.10].

So: casting for evoke's alternative cost and the later mandatory sacrifice are two different abilities on two different timings (cast trigger of the static ability at cast time, and the ETB trigger later) [702.74a], and nothing stops you from sacrificing the creature by other means in between, as long as some other sacrifice outlet is actually available.

question: if a card loses all abilities, does that include keyword abilities?
answer:
Yes. If a card or permanent loses all abilities, that includes any keyword abilities it has (such as flying, trample, deathtouch, etc.), because keyword abilities are simply a shorthand way of writing out an ability's full rules text — they are still abilities in every sense. Rule [702.1] explains that a keyword is just a name that stands in for rules text that would otherwise be written out on the card, and [702.1d] confirms that having a keyword ability is the same thing as having 'a [keyword ability] ability.' Since effects that remove abilities remove all instances of that ability [113.10], and 'loses all abilities' is a blanket removal, it strips away every ability the object has — named keywords included — not just abilities with fully spelled-out text.

One nuance: this only removes true abilities. If an effect merely defines a characteristic of the object (e.g., 'this creature is red') or states a quality without granting an ability (e.g., 'this creature can't be blocked'), that's not an ability being granted, per [113.12], so a 'loses all abilities' effect wouldn't strip those out — only genuine granted/printed abilities, including keywords, are affected.

question: can i draw cards if i'm already at my maximum hand size?
answer:
Yes. Maximum hand size doesn't stop you from drawing cards at any point during the game — it only matters at cleanup. There's no rule that prevents a draw just because you're already at (or above) your maximum hand size (normally seven, per rule [402.2]).

What maximum hand size actually does is trigger a discard during the cleanup step: immediately after the cleanup step begins, if the active player's hand contains more cards than their maximum hand size, they discard enough cards to get down to that number ([703.4n], [514.1]). This is a turn-based action that doesn't use the stack ([514.1]), and it's the active player's cleanup step specifically — non-active players aren't checked at that point.

So in practice: you can draw as many cards as an effect instructs, going arbitrarily above your maximum hand size, and nothing forces a discard mid-turn. The only time the excess matters is when your own cleanup step begins — at that point, if you're the active player and your hand is over the maximum (six, seven, or whatever your hand modifier sets it to, per [313.6] and [902.5b] for vanguard variants), you must discard down to it.

Note this reasoning assumes a normal two-player or multiplayer game with no special hand-size-altering effects other than what's cited; vanguard cards or other effects can change your specific maximum hand size number, but they don't change when the check happens.

question: what happens when a planeswalker has 0 or less loyalty counters?
answer:
A planeswalker with 0 loyalty counters is put into its owner's graveyard immediately, as a state-based action. This is confirmed directly by rule [306.9]: "If a planeswalker's loyalty is 0, it's put into its owner's graveyard," and reiterated by [704.5i] (which lists this as one of the state-based actions) and [122.1e] ("A planeswalker with 0 loyalty is put into its owner's graveyard as a state-based action").

Key background: Loyalty is a characteristic only planeswalkers have, represented by loyalty counters placed on the planeswalker while it's on the battlefield [306.5, 306.5c]. A planeswalker's loyalty can be reduced in two main ways: by paying a loyalty ability's cost that has a negative loyalty symbol, such as [-N], which means "Remove N loyalty counters from this permanent" [107.7]; or by taking combat/other damage, since damage dealt to a planeswalker causes that many loyalty counters to be removed from it rather than being marked as damage [306.8, 120.3c].

Because state-based actions (rule [704.1]) are checked continuously and applied automatically without using the stack, as soon as a planeswalker's loyalty-counter count reaches 0, that planeswalker is put into its owner's graveyard the next time state-based actions are checked (i.e., before any player would receive priority), with no player able to respond to stop it.

On "0 or less": the rules text you've provided only speaks in terms of a planeswalker's loyalty being exactly 0 [306.9, 704.5i, 122.1e]. There's no rule given here stating loyalty counters can go negative or describing a distinct 'less than 0' case, so based on what's provided, the effective floor is 0 and that's the trigger condition for going to the graveyard. If you're asking specifically whether loyalty can dip below zero (e.g., from a huge damage hit or a costly loyalty ability), the provided rules don't give an explicit answer to that sub-question, so I can't confirm that detail beyond noting the SBA fires at exactly 0.

This is a general rule that doesn't depend on player count — it applies the same whether there are two players or more than two players in the game; nothing in the multiplayer-specific rule provided [901.14b] changes how planeswalker loyalty or this state-based action works.

question: do non-creature artifacts die?
answer:
No. "Dies" is a defined game term that only applies to creatures and planeswalkers: rule [700.4] states "the term dies means 'is put into a graveyard from the battlefield,'" and the [Dies] keyword definition confirms this applies specifically to "a creature or planeswalker." A non-creature artifact (an artifact with no creature type, such as a plain Equipment or other artifact permanent) is neither a creature nor a planeswalker, so when it's put into its owner's graveyard from the battlefield, that event is not called "dying" — it's just going to the graveyard.

This matters practically for triggered abilities: an ability that says "whenever a creature dies" won't trigger off a non-creature artifact being destroyed or sacrificed, but an ability that says "whenever a permanent is put into a graveyard from the battlefield" or "whenever an artifact leaves the battlefield" would still apply to it.

Note the exception: if the artifact is also a creature (an artifact creature), rule [300.2] says such an object "combines the aspects of each of those card types," so it counts as a creature for this purpose — an artifact creature *does* die when it goes to the graveyard from the battlefield, just like any other creature.

Also relevant: a non-creature permanent has no power or toughness per rule [208.3], so the toughness-based state-based actions in [704.5f], [704.5g], and [704.5h] (which destroy or graveyard creatures based on toughness/damage) simply don't apply to it — a non-creature artifact can only leave the battlefield via effects like destroy, sacrifice, or bounce, not via lethal damage.

question: what happens if i should draw a card when my library is empty?
answer:
You don't lose the game instantly at the moment of the failed draw. Instead, that failed draw is remembered, and the game checks state-based actions the next time any player would receive priority — at that point you lose the game.

Specifically: attempting to draw a card from a library with no cards in it means you simply can't draw the card (there's nothing there to move to your hand). Rule [121.4] and [104.3c] state that a player who attempts to draw a card from an empty library loses the game the next time a player would receive priority, and [704.5b] confirms this is enforced as a state-based action: if a player has attempted to draw from an empty library since state-based actions were last checked, that player loses the game. Because state-based actions [704.1] don't use the stack, this loss is checked and applied before anyone gets to act, effectively as soon as priority would next be given out.

If you're required to draw more cards than remain in your library (e.g., 'draw three' but only one card is left), [104.3c] says you draw the remaining cards you can (here, the one card) and then lose the game the next time a player would receive priority — you don't get to draw zero, you draw what's available first.

Note that this only applies to actual 'draws.' If an effect moves cards from your library to your hand without using the word 'draw,' [121.5] says you haven't drawn those cards, so the empty-library-loss condition doesn't trigger from that. Also, replacement effects that replace a card draw still apply even if your library is empty ([121.6a], [614.11]) — so if something is replacing your draw, you don't fail to draw and the loss condition described above never gets triggered.

This works the same whether you're in a two-player game or a multiplayer game — the state-based action in [704.5b] just says 'that player loses the game' with no special multiplayer wording, so in multiplayer you'd simply be eliminated from the game while play continues among the remaining players, whereas in a two-player game your loss ends the game immediately.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming the draw attempt happens as a normal turn-based or effect-based draw (e.g., during your draw step, [504.1]/[121.1]) and that no replacement effect is intercepting it. If a replacement effect is in play, the outcome changes as noted above.

question: what are the steps in combat and when do I have priority as the defending player?
answer:
The combat phase has five steps, in order: beginning of combat, declare attackers, declare blockers, combat damage, and end of combat [506.1]. The declare blockers and combat damage steps are skipped entirely if no creatures are attacking [506.1].

As the defending player, you get priority in every step after that step's turn-based actions (and any resulting state-based actions) are completed, once the active player has had priority first and passes it to you. This is explicit for the end of combat step: it has no turn-based actions at all, and 'once it begins, the active player gets priority' [511.1] — meaning the active player acts first and then passes priority around the table, reaching you as the next player in turn order. In a two-player game 'the next player' is simply you, the defending player [506.2a].

Going step by step with the turn-based actions the rules give:
- Beginning of combat step: in a multiplayer game where opponents don't all automatically become defending players, the active player must first choose a defending player as a turn-based action [507.1] [703.4h]; in a two-player game there's no such choice to make [506.2]. After that turn-based action resolves, priority is passed starting with the active player, so you (the defending player) get priority once they pass it to you.
- Declare blockers step: you, the defending player, perform the turn-based action of declaring blockers first [509.1] [703.4j]. This declaration itself doesn't use the stack and you don't have priority while making it. Only after blockers are declared does priority get passed, again starting with the active player, then reaching you.
- Combat damage step: combat damage assignment (by attacking player, then defending player, per 510.1 [703.4k]) and the dealing of that damage [510.2] are both turn-based actions that don't use the stack, and 'no player has the chance to cast spells or activate abilities between the time combat damage is assigned and the time it's dealt' [510.2]. Priority only opens up after damage has actually been dealt, again active player first, then you.
- End of combat step: no turn-based actions; priority opens immediately, active player first, then you [511.1].

Multiplayer note: if the game has more than two opponents facing one active player, and the variant doesn't make all opponents defending players automatically, only the opponent chosen as defending player in the beginning of combat step [507.1][703.4h] gets the defending-player role and its associated turn-based actions (like declaring blockers). If instead the multiplayer variant makes all opponents defending players automatically (e.g., the Attack Multiple Players option) there is no such choice — all opponents are defending players together [802.1][802.2], and combat damage assignment then proceeds in APNAP order rather than just active-then-defending [802.5]. Other multiplayer options such as Attack Left/Right [803.1] or the Emperor variant [809.1] can also change who the defending player is, though the general priority pattern (active player first, then around the table) still applies. The rules given here don't spell out the exact generic 'active player always receives priority first in every step' rule outside of 511.1, so that pattern is drawn from the end-of-combat example and the turn-based-action ordering shown for the other steps.

question: can i respond to a mana ability?
answer:
No. Mana abilities never use the stack, so there is nothing to respond to. "Responding" (rule 117.7, defined under "Respond") means casting a spell or activating an ability while another spell or ability is on the stack, waiting to resolve. Mana abilities skip that entirely: an activated mana ability "resolves immediately after it is activated" [605.3b], and a triggered mana ability "resolves immediately after the mana ability that triggered it, without waiting for priority" [605.4a]. Because of this, rule [605.3b] explicitly states a mana ability "can't be targeted, countered, or otherwise responded to," and [113.4] confirms mana abilities "don't use the stack." [605.4a] repeats the same restriction for triggered mana abilities.

What you *can* do is activate your own mana abilities at almost any time, including in the middle of casting or resolving a spell or ability, per [605.3a] and [117.1d] — but that's you using a mana ability to generate mana for something, not responding to someone else's mana ability. Since a mana ability resolves the instant it's activated, there's no gap in which any player (even the ability's own controller) gets priority to interject something in reaction to it specifically [405.6c].

question: can I respond to a cost being paid?
answer: No. Paying a cost is not itself a stack action that other players can respond to. A cost (rule [118.1]) is just the action/payment a player carries out as part of casting a spell, activating an ability, or performing a turn-based action like declaring attackers or blockers — none of that goes on the stack, so no priority window opens during it. For example, declaring attackers and paying any associated costs is a turn-based action that "doesn't use the stack" ([508.1j]), and the same is true for declaring blockers and paying blocking costs ([509.1e], [509.1f]). Similarly, an activated ability's cost is paid as part of activating the ability, before the ability itself is put on the stack ([602.1], [118.2]). Only after the spell or ability is actually on the stack (or after a triggered ability triggers) do other players get a chance to respond — you can respond to the spell/ability that results from the cost being paid, but not to the moment of paying the cost itself. This holds the same way whether there are two players or more than two, since none of the rules describing cost-paying as a non-stack action differ by player count in the material provided.

question: can you explain layers?
answer:
The layer system is the process the game uses to figure out, in a fixed order, how all the continuous effects currently active on an object combine to determine its current characteristics (power, toughness, color, types, text, etc.). Rule [613.1] lays out the core idea: you start with the object's actual characteristics (for a card, the printed values; for a token or copy, the values set by the effect that created it) and then apply every applicable continuous effect in a series of layers, in a fixed order. Because the layers are applied in order, effects that change one kind of characteristic (say, color) can change how a later layer's effect behaves (say, a +1/+1 anthem that only affects white creatures).

The layers named in the provided rules include:
- Layer 1: Rules and effects that modify copiable values [613.1a], with sublayer 1a for copy effects and merging with permanents [613.2a].
- Layer 3: Text-changing effects [613.1c], governed by rule 612 [612.1].
- Layer 4: Type-changing effects (card type, subtype, supertype) [613.1d].
- Layer 5: Color-changing effects [613.1e].
- Layer 7: Power/toughness-changing effects, which itself has multiple sublayers applied in order [613.4] (the example in [613.5] shows sublayers 7b, setting P/T, and 7c, modifying P/T via counters, pumps, and static boosts).

Within a given layer or sublayer, if more than one effect applies, the game normally orders them by timestamp — the effect with the earlier timestamp is applied first [613.7]. However, if a dependency exists between two effects in the same layer/sublayer (one effect's outcome depends on whether/how the other effect has been applied), dependency overrides timestamp order [613.8], and this applies specifically within layer 1's sublayers [613.2] and layer 7's sublayers [613.4] as well.

An important wrinkle is that a single ability can generate an effect that spans multiple layers. Rule [613.6] explains that each part of such an effect is applied in its own appropriate layer, and once an effect starts applying to a set of objects it continues to do so in every relevant layer even if the source ability is later removed. The examples given: a spell that grants +1/+1 and changes color to your choice applies the color change in layer 5 and the +1/+1 in layer 7c; Act of Treason's control-change effect (layer 2, though not itemized in the given rules text beyond this example) and its haste-granting effect (layer 6) are applied separately; and Svogthos, the Restless Tomb's ability that makes it a creature with defined characteristics touches layers 4, 5, and 7b simultaneously.

Finally, rule [613.5] stresses that all of this is continually and automatically recalculated by the game as soon as an object's characteristics could be affected — the changes are instantaneous, not something a player manually tracks step by step, though understanding the layer order is what lets you correctly predict the result (as in the Honor of the Pure and Gray Ogre examples).

question: how does the legend rule work?
answer:
The legend rule is a state-based action: if a single player controls two or more legendary permanents that share the exact same name, that player must choose one of them to keep, and all the others go to their owners' graveyards. This is defined in [704.5j] and summarized under [Legend Rule]: "If two or more legendary permanents with the same name are controlled by the same player, that player chooses one of them, and the rest are put into their owners' graveyards."

Key points:
- It only applies to permanents that have the legendary supertype [205.4d]. Legendary instants/sorceries are not affected by the legend rule itself; instead they have a separate casting restriction requiring you to control a legendary creature or planeswalker [205.4e].
- The trigger is having the *same name*, not just being the same card or same legendary type. So if you control two permanents both named, say, "Kediss, Emberclaw Familiar," you'd have to sacrifice one to the legend rule (as a state-based action, this happens automatically the next time state-based actions are checked, before anyone gets priority).
- It's checked per player: only the permanents *you* control matter. If you and another player each control a legendary permanent with the same name, the legend rule does not apply, since it only triggers when the *same player* controls both duplicates.
- This applies to legendary creatures, legendary planeswalkers (planeswalkers were folded into this rule after the old "planeswalker uniqueness rule" was removed, per [306.4]), and any other legendary permanent type, since the legendary supertype is what matters, not the card type [205.4b].
- Legendary tokens created by an effect (per [111.9]) also carry the legendary supertype and are fully subject to the legend rule if their name matches another legendary permanent you control.

As for player count: the legend rule itself works identically whether you're in a two-player game or a multiplayer game, since it's defined purely in terms of "that player" controlling duplicates — it doesn't reference opponents or turn order at all, so no rules text here suggests any difference based on the number of players at the table.

Note that Commander formats (as described generally in [903.1]) don't change how the legend rule itself works, though commander deckbuilding relies on legendary cards.

question: when does my creature die after its been marked with a lethal amount of damage?
answer:
Your creature doesn't die the instant lethal damage is marked on it. Damage dealt to a creature by a source without wither or infect is marked on it [302.7], [120.3e], and it stays there [120.6]. Once the total damage marked on a creature is greater than or equal to its toughness, that creature "has been dealt lethal damage," which is defined as damage greater than or equal to its toughness [Lethal Damage]. Destruction then happens via a state-based action [704.5g], [704.5f is unrelated - that's for toughness 0 or less].

Crucially, damage itself never destroys the creature directly - the state-based action does [120.5]. State-based actions don't use the stack [704.1]; they're checked and applied automatically every time a player would receive priority, before that player actually gets priority [117.5], [117.2d]. So in practice, once combat damage (or any damage) is dealt and dealt simultaneously [703.4m], the very next time the game would give a player priority, it first checks state-based actions, sees the lethal damage marked on your creature, and destroys it right then - before any player can act on the new game state. There's also a special case: if an effect ends the turn, the game checks state-based actions as part of that process even without a player getting priority [724.1c].

So the short version: your creature dies as soon as the game next checks state-based actions, which for ordinary damage means essentially immediately after the damage is dealt (since that check happens before any priority is given), not later in the cleanup step. The damage itself simply sits marked on the creature [120.6] until it's removed by regeneration or during the cleanup step [514.2] - but the creature will already have been destroyed by the state-based action well before cleanup if the damage was lethal.

This doesn't depend on whether it's a two-player or multiplayer game - state-based action checking works the same way regardless of player count.

question: can I cast my commander from exile?
answer:
By default, no — your commander doesn't have blanket permission to be cast while sitting in exile just because it's your commander. Casting a spell requires either casting it from your hand, or having a specific rule or effect that lets you cast it from wherever it currently is [601.3f]. The Commander rules only grant an inherent "cast from a zone other than hand" permission for the command zone: rule [903.8] says "A player may cast a commander they own from the command zone," applying the commander tax of an additional {2} for each previous time it's been cast from the command zone that game. There's no equivalent blanket rule letting you cast a commander straight out of exile.

What usually happens instead: if your commander is in exile, rule [903.9a] is a state-based action — since the card was put into exile since the last time state-based actions were checked, you (its owner) may put it into the command zone. Once it's checked as a state-based action ([704.1]) and you choose to move it, it sits in the command zone and you can then cast it from there under [903.8] (paying the commander tax for however many times you've previously cast it from the command zone). Similarly, rule [903.9b] lets you redirect it to the command zone as a replacement effect if it would otherwise go to your hand or library from anywhere.

The exception: if some other rule or effect specifically gives you permission to cast a card from exile — for example, an adventure-cast permission after resolving as an Adventure [715.3d], a Plot ability letting you cast the plotted card from exile later [702.170d], or any 'you may cast this card from exile' effect — then you can cast your commander under that permission while it's still in exile, per [601.3f], and in that case it isn't being cast 'from the command zone,' so the commander tax from [903.8] wouldn't apply to that cast. If it's exiled face down, you'd also need to be allowed to look at it per [406.3b] to cast it.

So: check whether anything is letting the card be cast from exile specifically. If not, expect it to move to the command zone via the [903.9a] state-based action, and cast it from there instead.

question: what happens during the cleanup step?
answer:
The cleanup step is the second and final step of the ending phase (512.1, [Cleanup Step]). Two turn-based actions happen in it, and normally no player gets priority.

First, if the active player's hand contains more cards than their maximum hand size (normally seven), they discard enough cards to get down to that number. This discard doesn't use the stack [514.1] [703.4n].

Second, immediately after that discard (if any was needed), the following happen simultaneously as turn-based actions that don't use the stack: all damage marked on permanents (including phased-out permanents) is removed, and all "until end of turn" and "this turn" effects end [514.2] [703.4p] [120.6].

Normally, no player receives priority during the cleanup step, so no spells can be cast and no abilities can be activated [514.3] [514.3a]. This is one of the few steps that simply ends once its specified actions are completed, rather than ending because players pass priority in succession [500.3].

There is an exception: right after these actions, the game checks whether any state-based actions need to be performed or any triggered abilities are waiting to be put on the stack (this includes abilities that trigger "at the beginning of the next cleanup step"). If either is true, those state-based actions are performed, the triggered abilities go on the stack, and the active player then gets priority as normal — players may cast spells and activate abilities [514.3a] [704.3]. Once the stack is empty and all players pass in succession, another full cleanup step begins from the top (checking hand size again isn't needed since it's already been done, but damage/effects and the state-based-action/trigger check happen again) [514.3a]. If that new check finds nothing to do, the step simply ends without anyone getting priority [704.3].

This process is the same whether there are two players or more than two — the rules cited here don't vary cleanup by player count, though multiplayer games could still have more simultaneous triggers to sort out via the normal APNAP ordering when they go on the stack (not covered in the rules given here).

question: when are state-based actions checked?
answer:
State-based actions (SBAs) are automatically-occurring game actions—like a creature with 0 toughness dying or a player with 0 life losing—that don't use the stack and aren't controlled by any player [704.1, 704.1a, 704.2]. They are checked and performed every time a player would receive priority: the game first performs all applicable SBAs as a single simultaneous event, then repeats the check until none apply, then puts any waiting triggered abilities on the stack, and repeats the whole cycle until no more SBAs are performed and no triggers are waiting—only then does the appropriate player actually get priority [704.3, 117.5]. This means SBAs are dealt with *before* a player gets priority, not on some independent clock [117.2d, 405.6f]. 

A few important timing notes: 
- Turn-based actions (like the draw step's draw, or the cleanup step's discard-to-hand-size) are handled first when a step or phase begins, before SBAs are checked and before triggered abilities go on the stack [703.1, 703.3, 514.1, 117.3a]. 
- Normally no player gets priority during the cleanup step, but SBAs are still checked there: if the initial check finds an applicable SBA or a waiting triggered ability, those are performed/put on the stack and the active player then does get priority; otherwise the step just ends with no priority given [514.3a, 704.3]. 
- SBAs are checked continuously with respect to the game's actual current state, but they ignore anything that happens only transiently *during* the resolution of a spell or ability—they only look at the state that exists once a player would next get priority (i.e., after the spell/ability finishes resolving) [704.4]. 
- A few specific effects that end a phase outright (e.g., an effect that ends the combat phase) also force an SBA check as part of their own resolution steps, even though no priority is passed and no triggers go on the stack at that moment [724.2c]. 
- Some variant game formats add extra SBAs beyond the normal list, but the checking mechanism (whenever a player would get priority) is the same [704.6].

This all applies regardless of how many players are at the table—rule 704.3's "whenever a player would get priority" and rule 117.5's process aren't limited to two-player games, and none of the provided rules suggest a multiplayer-specific difference in *when* SBAs are checked.

question: how do I know who the active player is?
answer:
The active player is simply the player whose turn it currently is [102.1]. Every other player at the table is a nonactive player during that turn [102.1].

A few situational notes:
- If a player's turn is being controlled by someone else (for example, due to some effect), the player whose turn it actually is remains the active player even though another player is making the decisions [723.3].
- In a game using the shared team turns option, it's not an individual player but an entire team whose turn it is — that team is the 'active team,' and the other teams are nonactive teams [805.4a]. Within that active team, any player on it can be treated as 'the active player' for purposes like APNAP ordering [805.6].
- During the combat phase, the active player is also the attacking player — the one whose creatures may attack. In a two-player game, the other player is the defending player [506.2].

question: can I hold priority to cast more spells after I've cast one or more spells?
answer:
Yes. Whenever you have priority and cast a spell (or activate an ability, or take a special action), you get priority back immediately afterward, before any other player does — as long as no rule or effect gives priority to someone else first. This is often called "holding priority." You can keep doing this repeatedly: cast a spell, get priority back, cast another spell in response to the first, get priority back again, and so on, for as many spells/abilities as you're able to pay for and legally cast.

Mechanically: to cast a spell you move it to the stack and pay its costs (601.2a, 601.2f). Once that process is finished, "if the spell's controller had priority before casting it, they get priority" (601.2i; the same principle is stated generally at 117.3c: "If a player has priority when they cast a spell, activate an ability, or take a special action, that player receives priority afterward"). Each new spell you cast while something else is already on the stack is cast "in response to" the earlier spell/ability, and it will resolve first, on top of the stack (117.7). A phase or step only ends when the stack is empty and all players pass in succession (500.2), so nothing forces you to pass — you can keep adding spells to the stack until you're ready to stop.

Limits: you still need to actually be able to cast each spell — you need priority, the appropriate timing permissions (e.g., only instants can be cast when the stack isn't empty during most steps, per 304.1/117.1a), and you must be able to pay all costs, or the casting is illegal and gets reversed (601.3, 733.1).

Two-player vs. multiplayer: everything above is the general priority rule and isn't limited to two players — it applies at any table size. Two special multiplayer wrinkles are worth knowing: in team games, priority belongs to the team, not the individual, so any teammate (not just you) may act while your team has priority (805.5a). In the Grand Melee variant specifically, there are multiple stacks (one per turn marker), and if you have priority for more than one of them, you must specify which stack each new spell or ability goes on (807.5b) — the core "you get priority back after acting" rule still applies, but you're choosing among stacks rather than a single shared one.

question: when are lore counters put on sagas?
answer:
Lore counters get added to a Saga at two distinct times. First, when a Saga enters the battlefield, it gets its starting lore counter(s) as a replacement effect: a Saga without read ahead enters with one lore counter (rule 714.3a), while a Saga with read ahead enters with however many lore counters were chosen (between 1 and its final chapter number) as it entered (rules 714.3b, 702.155a/b). These are replacement effects (rule 614.1c) that modify the entering-the-battlefield event itself, not something that happens afterward.

Second, on every subsequent turn, immediately after the active player's precombat main phase begins, that player puts one additional lore counter on each Saga they control that has one or more chapter abilities (rules 505.4, 703.4f, 714.3c). This is a turn-based action, meaning it happens automatically without using the stack — it's not a triggered ability and can't be responded to before it happens (though the chapter ability it triggers does use the stack).

Note that a Saga's controller adds this counter, so in a multiplayer game each player independently adds a lore counter to their own Sagas at the start of their own precombat main phase — there's no single 'active player' effect that touches every player's Sagas at once; it only affects Sagas controlled by whichever player's precombat main phase is beginning. This is the same in two-player and multiplayer games, since the rule is stated per active player regardless of table size.

After lore counters are added, if a Saga's lore counter count is greater than or equal to its final chapter number (and it isn't currently the source of a chapter ability still on the stack), a state-based action causes its controller to sacrifice it (rules 714.4, 704.5s). This check happens continuously, not just once per turn.

question: what is a delayed triggered ability?
answer:
A delayed triggered ability is an ability that doesn't do anything right when it's created; instead, it triggers later on to do something at a specified future time. It's created (not immediately triggered) by an effect generated when a spell or ability resolves, when a replacement effect is applied, or when a static ability that allows a player to take an action is used. The ability's text will always contain the word "when," "whenever," or "at" somewhere (though not necessarily at the start), since that's what marks it as a triggered ability that will fire when its stated trigger event occurs.

Key points about how delayed triggered abilities work: they are created during the resolution of the spell/ability, or as a replacement effect is applied, or as a result of a static ability permitting an action (603.7a). A delayed triggered ability won't trigger until it has actually been created, even if its trigger event already happened just before that (603.7a) — for example, "When this creature leaves the battlefield" won't trigger if the creature already left before the effect creating it resolved. Normally, a delayed triggered ability triggers only once, the next time its trigger event happens, unless it has a stated duration like "this turn" (603.7b). It still affects a particular object it refers to even if that object changes characteristics, but not if that object has left the zone it's expected to be in (603.7c) — because an object that changes zones becomes a new object under rule 400.7. The source and controller of a delayed triggered ability depend on what created it: a triggering/activated ability that spawns one keeps the same source, with the controller being whoever controlled that ability as it resolved (603.7e); a spell that creates one has the spell itself as the source, with the controller being whoever controlled the spell as it resolved (603.7d); and static abilities that create them via replacement effects or granted actions have the permanent with that static ability as the source, with the controller matching that permanent's controller at the relevant time (603.7f, 603.7g).

A closely related concept is the reflexive triggered ability (603.12), which follows the same rules as delayed triggered abilities but is checked immediately after being created, based on whether its trigger event happened earlier in the resolution of the ability that created it (e.g., "When you do, ...").

Example from the provided card data: Earthbend N creates a delayed triggered ability as part of rule 701.66a ("When that land dies or is put into exile, return it to the battlefield tapped under your control"), and 701.66b confirms that any ability keying off "whenever a player earthbends" triggers when that delayed triggered ability is created.

question: can non-permanent spells have abilities?
answer: Yes. Non-permanent spells (instants and sorceries) can have abilities. Any text on an instant or sorcery spell is treated as a spell ability unless it is specifically an activated ability, a triggered ability, or a static ability that fits the exceptions listed in rule 113.6 [113.3a]. A spell ability is the kind of ability that's followed as instructions while the instant or sorcery spell resolves [Spell Ability, 113.3a]. As a general rule, abilities of an instant or sorcery spell function only while that spell is on the stack, with only the exceptions noted in rule 113.6 (for example, characteristic-defining abilities, which function in all zones per rule 604.3) letting an ability tied to a spell operate outside the stack [113.6, 604.3]. So while most rules text on an instant or sorcery is simply a spell ability that does its job during resolution, the card could in principle also carry an activated, triggered, or static ability, and abilities in general are able to affect the object they're on as well as other objects or players and can generate one-shot or continuous effects [113.2d, 113.1a].

question: can I use a mana ability when a spell with split-second is on the stack?
answer:
Yes. Even while a spell with split second is on the stack, you may still activate mana abilities. Split second's static ability says that as long as the spell is on the stack, players can't cast other spells or activate abilities that aren't mana abilities [702.61a], and rule [702.61b] explicitly confirms that players may activate mana abilities and take special actions while a split second spell is on the stack. Triggered abilities also still trigger and go on the stack normally during this window per [702.61b], but only if they are not mana abilities themselves — triggered mana abilities don't use the stack either [605.4a].

This works mechanically because mana abilities are a special category of ability that don't use the stack [113.4] and can be activated whenever you have priority, whenever you're casting a spell or activating an ability requiring a mana payment, or whenever a rule or effect asks for a mana payment — even mid-resolution of something else [605.3a], [117.1d]. Since they never go on the stack, they can't be responded to and resolve immediately upon activation [605.3b], [405.6c], so allowing them doesn't give opponents a way to 'respond' to the split second spell in any meaningful sense — it just lets players pay for things or generate mana as normal.

This holds the same way in a two-player game or in a multiplayer game, since nothing in the split second or mana ability rules provided distinguishes player count.
